item.text: {"question_id":"8B.3","answer":"Executed records show substantial, ruler-attributed mobilization toward selected priorities, but not consistently effective mobilization across the broader program portfolio. Under López Obrador, military institutions received 72.2% of security-institution spending in 2019–2023, military spending rose relative to 2018, the National Guard expanded, and military institutions trained thousands of commanders and tens of thousands of Guard personnel. These records demonstrate resource concentration and organizational buildup, not by themselves effective use or presidential personal direction (BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0055-E016). Social priorities also received major budgetary commitments: priority programs represented over 40% of social-program spending in 2023, and the older-adult pension expanded substantially in coverage, transfers, and exercised spending (BATCH-0052-E001; BATCH-0032-E006). However, implementation evidence is mixed. Four of 16 priority programs did not measure results, recommendations were disregarded to varying degrees, and half required better or additional result measurement; the four programs lacking clear result orientation or measurement represented a substantial budget share (BATCH-0052-E004; BATCH-0052-E006). Health-investment budgets were repeatedly under-executed, while large infrastructure and defense projects exceeded period allocations, indicating selective rather than uniformly effective mobilization (BATCH-0048-E010). Security mobilization likewise produced weak operational conversion: despite Guard expansion, local institutions performed nearly all prosecutor presentations and emergency-call responses, while Guard prosecutor presentations and narcotics seizures fell and armed confrontations rose (BATCH-0016-E008). Civilian oversight and transparency were limited, and major civilian functions were transferred to the armed forces despite concerns about supervision, procurement safeguards, and task fit (BATCH-0048-E012). The World Bank portfolio records further show mixed execution, including achieved and on-track objectives alongside off-track targets, cancellations, restructurings, institutional turnover, and changing priorities; these findings involve external shocks, partner institutions, and government choices, so they do not establish exclusive presidential causation (BATCH-0052-E015; BATCH-0052-E020). Overall, the evidence supports strong political direction and selective administrative mobilization, especially for militarization, transfers, and flagship projects, but only mixed effectiveness in converting those resources into monitored, coordinated, and reliably productive execution. Attribution is strongest to the administration's priorities and institutional configuration, weaker for individual agency performance, and not sufficient to attribute every outcome personally to López Obrador.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0016-E007","BATCH-0052-E001","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0055-E016","BATCH-0049-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0052-E004","BATCH-0052-E006","BATCH-0048-E010","BATCH-0016-E008","BATCH-0048-E012","BATCH-0052-E015","BATCH-0052-E020","BATCH-0013-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Budgets, staffing, training, and institutional output establish inputs or administrative activity, not necessarily effective mobilization or successful outcomes.","Several favorable records concern agencies, Congress, subnational bodies, or international partners and do not demonstrate personal presidential direction.","The evidence is strongest for security, transfers, infrastructure, and selected social programs;
